title: The Bus to the Mountains
subtitle: A brother and sister on a long bus ride — and all the ways to say how much of something there is.
description: An A2 reading and listening text about a bus trip into the North Carolina mountains, built around there is / there are and quantifiers (some, any, much, many, a few, a little).
passage: My name is Emma, and I love a long bus ride. My brother Jack always comes with me. Today we are on a big, noisy bus heading west from Charlotte to Asheville, up in the North Carolina mountains. Asheville is famous for its old houses, its cool summers and the flowers in its gardens. The road stretches out ahead of us, and I am excited.
Jack looks out of the window. "There's a lake down there," he says. "It's so blue."
"There are birds on it too," I say. "Look — three of them, near the far side."
"Is there a town near here where we can stop?" he asks.
I check the map. "There's a small one in about ten minutes. There aren't many houses — just a few farms and a lot of trees."
The bus pulls in next to a shop with a red roof. "Let's get some water and a snack," I say.
Jack looks in his bag and frowns. "I don't have any money with me."
"Isn't there any cash in your jacket? Check again."
He shakes his head. "There's none at all. I left my wallet at home."
I open my wallet and laugh. There are a lot of coins in it but only a few bills. "It's enough for both of us," I say. "Just don't order much."
"How much time do we have?" Jack asks.
"Not much. Ten minutes, maybe." I look out at the hills. "There are so many places to see up here, and we have so little time today. We can't stop everywhere."
Inside, we eat a sandwich at a small table by the window. The coffee smells good. "Are you having juice?" Jack asks.
"No, just water," I say. "I'll have coffee later."
Jack cannot sit still. He walks around the shop looking at the postcards and the jars of local honey.

Yesterday we stopped in a town called Hendersonville, which is famous for its apples. Jack asked me whether I had tried the cider. I hadn't, so we bought a bottle and shared it on a bench in the sun. It was cold and very sweet.
Suddenly Jack points out of the window. "There's a river over there!" The water is shining in the afternoon light.
"There's a lot of water in these mountains," I say. "Rivers, waterfalls, lakes — they're everywhere."

The driver sounds the horn and we grab our bags. As we climb back on board, I think about how much I like these trips. Tomorrow we will drive up to Mount Mitchell, the highest point east of the Mississippi. Today is already full of things worth remembering.

vocabulary.definition: used to say that something exists in a place: there IS a lake, there ARE birds
some in positive sentences, any in questions and negatives
much with uncountable nouns (much time), many with countable ones (many houses)
a few + countable (a few bills), a little + uncountable (a little water)
a piece of paper money (American English; British English: a note)
money as coins and bills, not a card
(of a vehicle) to stop at the side of the road
in the US, usually unfiltered apple juice, often sold at farms

exercises.title: There is / There are
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form. Look carefully at whether the noun is singular or plural.

items.explanation: 'Lake' is singular, so: there is (there's) a lake.
'Birds' is plural, so: there are birds.
Plural noun in a negative: there aren't many houses.

items.prompt: ___ a town near here where we can stop?
items.explanation: Singular question: Is there a town…?

items.prompt: ___ a lot of water in these mountains.
items.explanation: 'Water' is uncountable and takes the singular: there's a lot of water.

items.prompt: I don't have ___ money with me.
items.explanation: Use 'any' in a negative sentence; 'some' belongs in positive ones.

items.prompt: Let's get ___ water and a snack.
There are so ___ places to see up here.
There are a lot of coins but only ___ bills.
items.explanation: 'Bills' is countable, so 'a few'. 'A little' goes with uncountable nouns.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: The questions use different words from the text. Think about the meaning, not the exact wording.

items.prompt: Emma and Jack get on the bus in Charlotte. Where does it take them?
items.explanation: The bus is “heading west from Charlotte to Asheville, up in the North Carolina mountains”.

items.prompt: What kind of things bring visitors to Asheville?
options: Its architecture, its mild summers and its flowers
Its beaches and its warm sea
items.explanation: “Asheville is famous for its old houses, its cool summers and the flowers in its gardens.” Old houses are architecture, and cool summers are mild ones.

items.prompt: Why does Jack have to rely on his sister at the shop?
options: The shop will not take his card
He is not hungry or thirsty
items.explanation: “There's none at all. I left my wallet at home,” he says — so he has no money with him at all.

items.prompt: How would you describe the money in Emma's wallet?
options: Mostly small change, with very little paper money
A large amount of paper money
Nothing at all — only a bank card
items.explanation: “There are a lot of coins in it but only a few bills.” Bills are paper money.

items.prompt: What did Jack and Emma taste for the first time the day before?
items.explanation: Jack asked whether she had tried the cider: “I hadn't, so we bought a bottle and shared it on a bench in the sun.”

items.prompt: What is planned for the next day?
options: A drive up to the highest peak in the region
A bus ride to the beach
items.explanation: “Tomorrow we will drive up to Mount Mitchell, the highest point east of the Mississippi.”

discussion: Describe a long journey you have taken by bus, train or car. Who was with you?
Emma says there is never enough time to stop everywhere. How do you decide what to see when you visit a new place?
Look around the room you are in and describe it using 'there is' and 'there are' five times.
Write about 80 words describing a place in your country that is worth a long trip, and say why.
